edges.title: Zelter teaches Fanny Mendelssohn counterpoint and Bach

works.from: Carl Friedrich Zelter, composition lessons from 1819; letter to Goethe, 1816
works.to: Fanny Mendelssohn playing the 24 preludes of the Well-Tempered Clavier from memory (1819)

edges.claim: [[fanny-hensel]] and her brother [[mendelssohn]] received composition lessons from Carl Friedrich Zelter, head of the Berlin Sing-Akademie, starting in 1819; Ludwig Berger had earlier taught them piano. In 1816 Zelter had written to Goethe that her father’s eldest daughter “could give you something of Sebastian Bach”. At fourteen she played all twenty-four preludes of the Well-Tempered Clavier from memory for her father’s birthday in 1819.

sources.title: Fanny Hensel (Wikipedia): education, Zelter, the Well-Tempered Clavier

edges.title: Chopin hears village musicians at Szafarnia, 1825

works.from: Folk songs and dances of the Dobrzyń land, heard at Szafarnia, summers 1824 and 1825
works.to: Chopin’s mazurkas, from Op. 6 and Op. 7 (composed 1830–31, published 1832)

edges.claim: [[chopin]] spent the summers of 1824 and 1825 at Szafarnia, the Dziewanowski estate, where he met authentic folk music at first hand: he wrote down songs he heard, joined in rural amusements, and in a letter home of 26 August 1825 describes accompanying a fiddler on a one-stringed cello. His first published mazurkas, Op. 6 and Op. 7, date from 1830–31 and appeared in 1832. In 1852 [[liszt]] wrote that Chopin’s mazurkas grew directly out of Polish national music, and later writers read “national” as “folk”; recent scholarship holds instead that the likelier source is the national music Chopin heard in the towns.
edges.note: The Szafarnia summers are documented in Chopin’s own letters. Whether the mazurkas rest directly on village folk music, as Liszt’s 1852 book was read to say, or on the urban national music of Warsaw, is debated; the evidence does not settle which tunes, if any, he took from what he heard in 1824–25.

sources.title: Szafarnia (Fryderyk Chopin, Great Composers, Narodowy Instytut Fryderyka Chopina)
sources.locator: letter of 26 August 1825; folk music at Szafarnia

edges.title: Mendelssohn reads Shakespeare in German and writes an overture

works.from: Shakespeare, A Midsummer Night’s Dream, in the Schlegel–Tieck German translation
works.to: Mendelssohn, Overture, Op. 21 (finished 6 August 1826); incidental music, Op. 61 (1842–43)

edges.claim: After reading August Wilhelm Schlegel’s German translation of A Midsummer Night’s Dream, made with Ludwig Tieck’s help, [[mendelssohn]] finished the concert overture, Op. 21, on 6 August 1826, at seventeen years and six months. It was first played at Stettin on 20 February 1827. In 1843 he added the incidental music for a Potsdam production, first performed on 14 October, and incorporated the overture; that score includes the Wedding March.

edges.title: Chopin varies Mozart’s Là ci darem; Schumann cheers

works.from: Mozart, Don Giovanni, Act I duet “Là ci darem la mano” (1787)
works.to: Chopin, Variations on “Là ci darem la mano”, Op. 2, piano and orchestra (1827)

edges.claim: At seventeen [[chopin]] wrote a set of variations for piano and orchestra on the duet sung by Don Giovanni and Zerlina in [[mozart]]’s opera, and dedicated it to his schoolfriend Tytus Woyciechowski; it was published in 1830. [[schumann]], who practised it for months, answered it through his alter ego Eusebius in the Allgemeine musikalische Zeitung of 7 December 1831 with the cry “Hats off, gentlemen”. Chopin’s own view of the Leipzig reviews was cooler: of Friedrich Wieck’s notice in Caecilia he wrote that Wieck, “instead of being clever, is very stupid”.

edges.title: Berlioz sees Hamlet at the Odéon, 1827

works.from: Hamlet and Romeo and Juliet, Odéon, Paris, 11 and 15 September 1827
works.to: Roméo et Juliette, Op. 17 (1839); Béatrice et Bénédict (1862)

edges.claim: On 11 September 1827 [[berlioz]] saw Hamlet at the Odéon with Harriet Smithson as Ophelia; on 15 September he saw her as Juliet. He calls the evening, in the Mémoires (chapter 18), the “greatest drama” of his life and says Shakespeare, arriving unawares, struck him like a thunderbolt. He married Smithson in 1833, and the plays stayed with him: Roméo et Juliette (1839) and Béatrice et Bénédict (1862, after Much Ado About Nothing) are the largest results.

edges.title: Berlioz hears Habeneck’s Beethoven at the Conservatoire

works.from: Beethoven’s symphonies, Société des concerts du Conservatoire (first concert 9 March 1828)
works.to: Symphonie fantastique, Op. 14 (premiere 5 December 1830)

edges.claim: The Société des concerts du Conservatoire, directed by François Habeneck, gave its first concert on 9 March 1828, and from then on Paris heard [[beethoven]]’s symphonies played regularly. In his Mémoires (chapter 20) [[berlioz]] says the shock was almost equal to Shakespeare’s: Beethoven opened a new world in music as the poet had opened one in poetry. From 1828 he also studied and copied Beethoven’s scores in the Conservatoire library. Two years later Habeneck conducted the premiere of the Symphonie fantastique in the same hall.

edges.title: Mendelssohn conducts the St Matthew Passion, Berlin, 1829

works.from: Bach, St Matthew Passion, BWV 244
works.to: Mendelssohn’s revival, Berlin Sing-Akademie, 11 March 1829

edges.claim: [[mendelssohn]]’s grandmother Bella Salomon had given him a copy of the St Matthew Passion score in the mid-1820s, and his teacher Carl Friedrich Zelter, head of the Sing-Akademie, held a store of Bach scores but would not perform the work in public. On 11 March 1829, aged twenty, Mendelssohn conducted the Passion at the Sing-Akademie in Berlin, the first performance outside Leipzig. He cut about a third of the arias and half the choruses but few chorales, and the revival is usually counted as the start of the Bach revival.

edges.title: Berlioz reads Nerval’s Faust and sets eight scenes

works.from: Goethe, Faust Part One, in Gérard de Nerval’s French translation (1828)
works.to: Huit scènes de Faust (1828–29); La damnation de Faust (1846)

edges.claim: [[berlioz]] first read Goethe’s Faust in Gérard de Nerval’s prose translation and says in the Mémoires (chapter 26) that he could not put it down, reading it at table, in the theatre and in the street. He set the translation’s verse fragments as Huit scènes de Faust, had them engraved at his own expense in 1829, then collected and destroyed the copies; the “Concert des Sylphes” was sung at his Conservatoire concert of 1 November 1829. Twenty years later he reworked those ideas into La damnation de Faust, first given at the Opéra-Comique on 6 December 1846.

edges.title: Schumann’s Papillons retell the masked ball in Flegeljahre

works.from: Jean Paul, Flegeljahre (1804–05), final masked-ball chapters
works.to: Schumann, Papillons, Op. 2 (1829–31)

edges.claim: In April 1832 [[schumann]] explained to the editor Ludwig Rellstab how his Papillons arose: he asked him to recall the last scene of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre, the masked ball, the dancing, the exchange of masks, the confessions and the brother’s departure. He said he kept turning to the last page, “almost unconsciously” found himself at the piano, and one piece after another came into being. In November 1829 he had written to Friedrich Wieck that Schubert was “my only Schubert” just as Jean Paul was “my only Jean Paul”.

sources.title: Notes to Schumann: Papillons, Op. 2 (Hyperion): letter of April 1832 to Ludwig Rellstab; letter of November 1829 to Friedrich Wieck

edges.title: Liszt hears Paganini at the Opéra, April 1832

works.from: Paganini, benefit concert at the Paris Opéra, 22 April 1832; Caprices Op. 1
works.to: Liszt, Études d’exécution transcendante d’après Paganini (1838); Grandes études de Paganini (1851)

edges.claim: [[liszt]], not yet twenty-one, first heard Paganini on 22 April 1832 at an Opéra benefit for victims of the cholera epidemic (some sources give 20 April). On 2 May he wrote to Pierre Wolff that he was practising exercises “four or five hours” a day and studying a long shelf of authors and composers at once. The first result was the Grande fantaisie de bravoure sur La Clochette (1832); the six Paganini études were published in 1838 and revised in 1851, with five of them based on Paganini’s Caprices.

edges.title: Chopin dedicates his Op. 10 études to Liszt

works.from: Chopin, 12 Études, Op. 10 (1833), “à mon ami Franz Liszt”
works.to: Liszt playing the Op. 10 études (joint letter to Hiller, June 1833)

edges.claim: [[chopin]] dedicated his twelve Op. 10 études, published in 1833, “to my friend Franz Liszt”; the second set, Op. 25, went to Liszt’s companion Marie d’Agoult. That June, in a letter to Ferdinand Hiller, Chopin wrote that he did not know what his pen was scribbling because Liszt was playing his études at that moment, and that he wished he could steal from Liszt the way to play them.

edges.title: Paganini’s viola request becomes Byron’s Harold in Italy

works.from: Byron, Childe Harold’s Pilgrimage (1812–18)
works.to: Harold en Italie, Op. 16, for viola and orchestra (premiere 23 November 1834)

edges.claim: Paganini asked [[berlioz]] for a showpiece for his Stradivari viola, then rejected the first movement because the viola rested too long. Berlioz kept the plan but made the solo a “melancholy dreamer in the manner of Byron’s Childe Harold”, set among his memories of the Abruzzi, and named the symphony Harold en Italie. As in the Fantastique, a theme recurs, but the viola theme is laid over the orchestra’s tunes instead of interrupting them; the first performance was at the Conservatoire on 23 November 1834.

edges.title: Mendelssohn learns Chopin’s new nocturne by ear

works.from: Chopin, Nocturne in D♭, Op. 27 No. 2, played at Friedrich Wieck’s house, Leipzig, September 1835
works.to: Mendelssohn’s letter to his sister Fanny

edges.claim: In September 1835 [[chopin]] visited Leipzig, where he played at Friedrich Wieck’s house and met both [[schumann]] and [[mendelssohn]]. He played the D♭ Nocturne, which was then new; Mendelssohn wrote to his sister [[fanny-hensel]] that Chopin “has also such a lovely new notturno, a considerable part of which I learnt by ear”. The two Op. 27 nocturnes were published the following year in Leipzig, Paris and London.

edges.title: Mendelssohn conducts Clara Wieck’s piano concerto, 1835

works.from: Mendelssohn conducting the Leipzig Gewandhaus Orchestra, 9 November 1835
works.to: Clara Wieck, Piano Concerto in A minor, Op. 7 (1833–35)

edges.claim: Clara Wieck began her Piano Concerto at thirteen, in January 1833. Robert Schumann revised the orchestration of its first movement in 1834; she later undid his changes, orchestrated it herself, and finished the three-movement concerto on 1 September 1835, twelve days before her sixteenth birthday. [[mendelssohn]] conducted the Leipzig Gewandhaus Orchestra at the first performance of the complete work on 9 November 1835, with Clara as soloist.

edges.title: Schumann hides a Beethoven song in his Fantasie

works.from: Beethoven, An die ferne Geliebte, Op. 98 (1816), last song “Nimm sie hin denn, diese Lieder”
works.to: Schumann, Fantasie in C, Op. 17, first movement, closing bars (1836; published 1839)

edges.claim: [[schumann]] began the Fantasie in 1836 as Ruines, a piece written in his distress at being parted from Clara Wieck. He expanded it into a work to raise money for the Beethoven monument in Bonn, offering 100 presentation copies to the publisher Kistner. The last bars of the first movement quote the phrase “Nimm sie hin denn, diese Lieder” (“Accept, then, these songs”) from [[beethoven]]’s song cycle, a quotation Schumann did not acknowledge and which apparently went unnoticed until 1910. He dedicated the published score, of 1839, to [[liszt]].

edges.title: Liszt puts all nine Beethoven symphonies on the piano

works.from: Beethoven, Symphonies Nos. 1–9
works.to: Liszt, Symphonies de Beethoven, S. 464 (Nos. 5–7 by 1837; the nine complete in 1865)

edges.claim: [[liszt]] began transcribing the Fifth Symphony around the end of 1835, and by mid-1837 had finished Nos. 5, 6 and 7 for solo piano; the Fifth and Sixth were published in 1840 with a dedication to the painter Ingres. After twenty-three years Breitkopf & Härtel asked him to go on, and the nine appeared together in 1865, dedicated to Hans von Bülow. He had made a two-piano version of the Ninth in 1850 and at first doubted that its finale could be arranged effectively for one piano.

edges.title: Chopin sings Bellini’s line at the piano

works.from: Bellini, I puritani (1835), march “Suoni la tromba”; the bel canto vocal line
works.to: Chopin, Variation VI (Largo) in Hexaméron (1837); Nocturne in D♭, Op. 27 No. 2 (1835)

edges.claim: Bellini’s friendship with [[chopin]] dates from his stay in Paris, which began in 1833. On 31 March 1837 Chopin contributed the Largo sixth variation to Hexaméron, the set of variations on “Suoni la tromba” from I puritani that Princess Belgiojoso commissioned from six pianists for a benefit in her Paris salon. Chopin told pupils to study the great opera singers and to imitate them, and a programme note on the Op. 27 nocturnes hears a “bel canto melody over rippling broken chords” in the D♭ Nocturne.

edges.title: Clara’s mazurka opens Schumann’s Davidsbündlertänze

works.from: Clara Wieck, Soirées musicales, Op. 6, No. 5, Mazurka (1836)
works.to: Schumann, Davidsbündlertänze, Op. 6, No. 1, “Motto by C. W.” (1837)

edges.claim: Clara Wieck and [[schumann]] became secretly engaged on 14 August 1837, against her father’s opposition; within a week he began the Davidsbündlertänze. The opening bars, headed “Motto by C. W.”, quote the start of the mazurka that is No. 5 of her Soirées musicales, Op. 6, and he began to sketch a whole piece on her theme. Schumann later said that these pieces were more urgently addressed to her than anything else he had written; the published set is inscribed to Walther von Goethe, the poet’s grandson.

edges.title: Clara Wieck plays Beethoven; Grillparzer writes a poem

works.from: Beethoven, Piano Sonata in F minor, Op. 57 (“Appassionata”)
works.to: Clara Wieck’s Vienna concerts, December 1837–April 1838; Grillparzer, “Clara Wieck und Beethoven” (January 1838)

edges.claim: Clara Wieck reached Vienna in December 1837 and, once sure of her audience, added Chopin, Bach and Beethoven to her programmes, which was rare then. Her playing of Beethoven’s Appassionata moved the poet Franz Grillparzer to write “Clara Wieck und Beethoven” in January 1838. [[schumann]] called it the most beautiful poem ever written about her and printed it in the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik that month.

edges.title: Hoffmann’s mad Kapellmeister becomes Schumann’s Kreisleriana

works.from: E. T. A. Hoffmann, “Kreisleriana”, Fantasy Pieces in Callot’s Manner (1814–15); Kater Murr
works.to: Schumann, Kreisleriana, Op. 16 (1838)

edges.claim: [[schumann]]’s eight Kreisleriana take their title from Johannes Kreisler, the eccentric, wild and witty Kapellmeister in E. T. A. Hoffmann’s Fantasy Pieces in Callot’s Manner and in Kater Murr. Schumann told Clara in 1838 that she and one of her ideas played the main role in the work, and that he wanted to dedicate it to her alone; the printed dedication is to Chopin. He said he wrote it in four days in April 1838, a claim one biographer dates differently, to between May and September.

edges.title: Paganini’s 20,000 francs pay for Roméo et Juliette

works.from: Paganini’s letter and gift, Paris, 18 December 1838
works.to: Roméo et Juliette, Op. 17 (first given 24 November 1839)

edges.claim: Paganini, by then voiceless, heard Harold en Italie for the first time at [[berlioz]]’s Conservatoire concert of 16 December 1838, and had his son Achille relay his admiration. Two days later he wrote that with Beethoven dead only Berlioz could revive him, and sent 20,000 francs through the Baron de Rothschild. The money cleared Berlioz’s debts and left him free to compose: Roméo et Juliette was given three times, on 24 November, 1 and 15 December 1839.

edges.title: Chopin finishes 24 Preludes with Bach’s Forty-Eight at hand

works.from: Bach, The Well-Tempered Clavier (24 preludes and fugues in each of two books)
works.to: Chopin, 24 Préludes, Op. 28 (1835–39; published 1839)

edges.claim: [[chopin]] spent the winter of 1838–39 at Valldemossa, Majorca, where he had a copy of the Well-Tempered Clavier and finished his Op. 28 preludes, a cycle through all twenty-four keys. He ordered them differently from Bach, by the circle of fifths with each major key followed by its relative minor, and wrote no fugues. Jean-Jacques Eigeldinger’s study of Chopin’s markings in the WTC copy of his pupil Pauline Chazaren shows that by 1838 he knew a Paris edition of the work thoroughly.

edges.title: Wagner attends Berlioz’s Roméo et Juliette in Paris

works.from: Berlioz, Roméo et Juliette, third performance, Paris Conservatoire, 15 December 1839
works.to: Wagner’s article on Berlioz (Dresdner Abendzeitung, May 1841); Tristan inscription (1860)

edges.claim: On 15 December 1839 [[wagner]], newly arrived in Paris, was present at the third performance of Roméo et Juliette at the Conservatoire, conducted by [[berlioz]]; the programme also had two movements of Harold en Italie and a movement of the Requiem. In May 1841 Wagner published an article that had a great deal to say about Berlioz, and in early 1860 he sent Berlioz the score of Tristan inscribed to “the dear and great author of Romeo and Juliet”, from “the grateful author of Tristan”. The editor of the Berlioz website takes the inscription as Wagner’s open acknowledgement of Berlioz’s influence on his work.

edges.title: Schumann finds Schubert’s Great C major in Vienna

works.from: Schubert, Symphony in C major, D. 944 (“Great”, 1825–26), manuscript held by his brother Ferdinand
works.to: Schumann’s copy sent to Leipzig; first complete performance, Gewandhaus, 21 March 1839, conducted by Mendelssohn

edges.claim: The Gesellschaft der Musikfreunde in Vienna, to whom Schubert had sent the score, tried it briefly and rejected it for its length and difficulty. In January 1839 [[schumann]] visited Schubert’s brother Ferdinand in Vienna and discovered a copy of the manuscript among the composer’s papers; he took a copy back to Leipzig and sent it to [[mendelssohn]], who conducted the first complete public performance with the Gewandhaus Orchestra on 21 March 1839. Schumann’s article in the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik praised the symphony’s “heavenly length”, likening it to a four-volume novel, perhaps by Jean Paul.

edges.title: Did Mickiewicz’s poems inspire Chopin’s Ballades?

works.from: Adam Mickiewicz, Ballady i romanse (1822) and Konrad Wallenrod (1828)
works.to: Chopin, Ballades Nos. 1–4 (No. 1, Op. 23, composed 1835–36)

edges.claim: In 1841 Robert Schumann reported in the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik that [[chopin]] had told him poems by the Polish poet Adam Mickiewicz inspired his ballades. Chopin left no statement of his own, and Schumann’s remark concerned the second Ballade in particular. A tradition links the first Ballade with Konrad Wallenrod, a poem about a Lithuanian raised among the Teutonic Knights who leads them to defeat; no document ties either piece to a particular poem. When Schumann visited Leipzig in 1836 he told Chopin that the G minor Ballade was his favourite of Chopin’s works, and Chopin replied that it was his too.
edges.note: Schumann’s 1841 report that Mickiewicz inspired the Ballades is documented; Chopin never named a poem, Schumann’s remark was “far from specific”, and the match of Ballade No. 1 with Konrad Wallenrod is a later tradition. Which poems, if any, stand behind which Ballade is unresolved.

works.from: Wilhelm Hensel, pen vignettes for each month, in the manuscript of Das Jahr (1842)

edges.claim: [[fanny-hensel]] composed Das Jahr, twelve piano pieces depicting the months, in 1841 and gave it to her husband, the painter Wilhelm Hensel, as a Christmas present. They then reworked it together: the music was written on tinted paper, Wilhelm drew a vignette into the score for each month, and each piece carries a short poem by a German poet. The image shown is the opening of April.

works.from: Mendelssohn’s invitation and Gewandhaus concerts, Leipzig, February 1843
works.to: Berlioz’s Gewandhaus concerts of 4 and 22 February 1843

edges.claim: [[mendelssohn]] had been [[berlioz]]’s guide in Rome in 1831: each morning he played a Beethoven sonata, Berlioz wrote home, and they sang Gluck’s Armide. It was through Mendelssohn that Berlioz was invited to Leipzig in 1843, where he gave Gewandhaus concerts on 4 and 22 February. The two exchanged batons “as a token of friendship”, but Berlioz noted that Mendelssohn praised his romances and said nothing of the symphonies, overtures or Requiem.

edges.title: Schumann writes six fugues on B–A–C–H, 1845

works.from: Bach, third subject of the unfinished fugue of The Art of Fugue (B♭–A–C–B♮)
works.to: Schumann, Six Fugues on the name BACH, Op. 60 (organ or pedal piano), 1845

edges.claim: Both [[schumann]] and [[liszt]] wrote works on the four-note motif that spells Bach’s name in German notation, and both helped found the Bach-Gesellschaft in 1850. Schumann finished his Six Fugues on the name BACH in November 1845, calling them the work that would, he believed, outlive his others, and saying he had tried to make them worthy of the great name they bear. The first fugue introduces the four notes slowly and builds from a sombre exposition; the second compresses the subject and adds Baroque semiquaver figures.

edges.title: Wagner conducts Beethoven’s Ninth in Dresden, 1846

works.from: Beethoven, Symphony No. 9, Op. 125
works.to: Wagner’s Dresden performance, Palm Sunday, 5 April 1846; Bayreuth foundation-stone concert, 1872

edges.claim: [[wagner]] made a piano transcription of Beethoven’s Ninth in 1830, aged seventeen. On Palm Sunday, 5 April 1846, he conducted it in Dresden, where Robert Schumann was living and, on Christopher Reynolds’s evidence, also studying the work: both composers took from it a more contrapuntal, motivic style, and Reynolds points to Beethoven’s gradual build-up of the “Ode to Joy” melody. Wagner conducted the Ninth again to inaugurate the Bayreuth Festspielhaus, whose foundation stone was laid on 22 May 1872.

sources.title: Christopher Alan Reynolds, Wagner, Schumann, and the Lessons of Beethoven’s Ninth (University of California Press, 2015)
sources.locator: publisher’s description: Dresden 1845–46; performance on Palm Sunday 1846

edges.title: Verdi sets Macbeth, his first Shakespeare opera

works.from: Shakespeare, Macbeth (c. 1606)
works.to: Verdi, Macbeth, premiere 14 March 1847, Florence; revised French version, 21 April 1865, Paris

edges.claim: [[verdi]]’s Macbeth, first given at the Teatro della Pergola in Florence on 14 March 1847, was the first Shakespeare play he adapted for the stage. He told his librettist Piave that the tragedy was “one of the greatest creations of man” and that if they could not make something great of it they should at least make something out of the ordinary. In 1865 he wrote that Shakespeare was “one of my favorite poets”, whom he had had “in my hands from my earliest youth”. For the revised version, given in French in Paris on 21 April 1865, he insisted that the Witches rule the drama.

sources.title: Macbeth (Verdi) (Wikipedia): composition, letters to Piave and of 1865, revision

edges.title: From Berlioz’s Witches’ Sabbath to Liszt’s Totentanz

works.from: Berlioz, Symphonie fantastique, V: Dies irae from bar 127, bassoons and ophicleides (1830)
works.to: Liszt, Totentanz: Paraphrase on Dies irae, S. 126, piano and orchestra (completed 1849)

edges.claim: In the finale of the Symphonie fantastique, Berlioz gives the Dies irae chant to four bassoons and two ophicleides in C minor from bar 127, a funeral rite turned into a parody at the witches’ sabbath. [[liszt]] met Berlioz the day before the premiere on 5 December 1830 and in 1833 made the piano transcription of the symphony. His Totentanz, planned in 1838, completed in 1849 and revised in 1853 and 1859, is a set of variations for piano and orchestra on the same chant. A second recorded source is the Triumph of Death fresco in the Campo Santo at Pisa, which Liszt saw in 1838.
edges.note: Both works are documented; no letter or statement has been found in which Liszt names the Fantastique as the source of the Dies irae idea. He knew the symphony intimately, but the Pisa fresco is the other recorded stimulus for the Totentanz.

sources.title: The Hector Berlioz Website: Symphonie fantastique (form of the fifth movement, bars 127–221)

edges.title: Liszt conducts Lohengrin while Wagner is in exile

works.from: Liszt’s Weimar production, Court Theatre, 28 August 1850
works.to: Wagner, Lohengrin, WWV 75

edges.claim: [[wagner]] had fled Saxony after the May 1849 uprising in Dresden, in which he took part, and could not attend the first production of Lohengrin. [[liszt]] conducted it at Weimar on 28 August 1850, a date he chose to honour Goethe, who was born there in 1749; David Trippett’s study calls the decision politically as well as artistically risky for the Weimar court. Wagner did not see a complete performance until Vienna in 1861; in the meantime he conducted extracts in Zürich, London, Paris and Brussels.

edges.title: Verdi sees La Dame aux camélias and writes Traviata

works.from: Alexandre Dumas fils, La Dame aux camélias (novel 1848; play, Paris, 1852)
works.to: Verdi, La traviata, Venice, 6 March 1853; Act I prelude

edges.claim: In February 1852 [[verdi]] and Giuseppina Strepponi attended a performance in Paris of Alexandre Dumas fils’s La Dame aux camélias, a play adapted from his own 1848 novel. His biographer Mary Jane Phillips-Matz reports that he began composing at once, though Julian Budden notes that Verdi had probably read the book earlier. Francesco Maria Piave wrote the libretto, and La traviata was first performed at La Fenice, Venice, on 6 March 1853.

edges.title: Did Brahms fall asleep during Liszt’s B minor Sonata?

works.from: Liszt, Piano Sonata in B minor, S. 178 (completed 1853), played at Weimar
works.to: Brahms’s visit to Weimar with Ede Reményi, June 1853

edges.claim: In 1853 [[brahms]] and the violinist Ede Reményi visited Weimar, where Brahms met [[liszt]], Peter Cornelius and Joachim Raff, and Liszt played Brahms’s Scherzo, Op. 4, at sight. Reményi later claimed that Brahms then slept while Liszt played his own B minor Sonata. This and other disagreements led Reményi and Brahms to part company; that autumn Brahms went instead to the Schumanns in Düsseldorf.
edges.note: The only source for Brahms sleeping through the Sonata is Reményi’s account, written long afterwards and given by Brahms’s biographers as a claim. Liszt’s sight-reading of the Scherzo and the Weimar meetings are recorded; the Sonata was dedicated to Schumann and published only in 1854.

sources.title: Johannes Brahms (Wikipedia): Weimar visit with Reményi

edges.title: Schumann’s “Neue Bahnen” launches the 20-year-old Brahms

works.from: Schumann, “Neue Bahnen”, Neue Zeitschrift für Musik, 28 October 1853
works.to: Brahms’s first publications (Opp. 1–6) and his ties to Robert and Clara Schumann

edges.claim: In October 1853, with a letter of introduction from Joseph Joachim, the twenty-year-old [[brahms]] called on the Schumanns in Düsseldorf and played his works from memory. Robert is said to have broken off to fetch Clara, saying she must hear music “as you have never heard it before”; she noted in her diary that the visitor seemed “specially sent by God”. On 28 October [[schumann]] published “Neue Bahnen” in the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik, naming Brahms as the one fated to give the age its highest and most ideal expression; publishers began to take an interest at once.

edges.title: Wagner finds Schopenhauer and plans Tristan, 1854

works.from: Schopenhauer, Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung (1819; 2nd ed. 1844)
works.to: Wagner, Tristan und Isolde (composed 1857–59); letter to Liszt, 16 December 1854

edges.claim: On 16 December 1854 [[wagner]] wrote from Zürich to [[liszt]] that he had been absorbed in a “gift from heaven”, Arthur Schopenhauer, “the greatest philosopher since Kant”; the poet Georg Herwegh had urged him to read The World as Will and Representation. In the same letter he announces Tristan und Isolde: never having known the true bliss of love, he would “erect a monument to the most beautiful of all my dreams”, a conception he calls the simplest but most full-blooded imaginable, ending under a black flag. The first musical sketches date from 19 December 1856, and on 9 August 1857 he broke off Siegfried to compose it.

sources.title: Wagner to Liszt, Zürich, 16 December 1854 (English text, The Wagnerian)

edges.title: Brahms varies the same Schumann theme as Clara

works.from: Schumann, Bunte Blätter, Op. 99, No. 4 (1838–41); Clara Schumann, Variations Op. 20 (1853)
works.to: Brahms, Variations on a Theme by Robert Schumann, Op. 9 (May–June and September 1854)

edges.claim: [[brahms]] wrote his Op. 9 variations in Düsseldorf in May and June 1854, with variations 10 and 11 added in September, while Robert Schumann was confined in the asylum at Endenich near Bonn. He took the theme from the fourth piece of Schumann’s Bunte Blätter, Op. 99, the same theme that [[clara-schumann]] had chosen for her own variations, Op. 20, in 1853. Clara is the dedicatee, and Brahms brought each variation to show her as he wrote it.

sources.title: Notes to Brahms: Variations on a theme by R Schumann, Op 9 (Hyperion)

edges.title: Brahms signs against Wagner’s party, then helps Wagner

works.from: The New German School’s organ, Brendel’s Neue Zeitschrift für Musik; Wagner’s Vienna concerts of 1862–63
works.to: The 1860 manifesto, almost certainly drafted by Brahms; Brahms’s help with Wagner’s concerts

edges.claim: In 1860 a manifesto against the “pursuits of a certain party” whose organ was Brendel’s Neue Zeitschrift für Musik circulated with the signatures of [[brahms]], Joseph Joachim and others; its author was almost certainly Brahms. It leaked, the Neue Zeitschrift parodied it on 4 May, and it appeared in the Echo on 6 May with more than twenty names. Yet in Vienna Brahms helped prepare [[wagner]]’s concerts of 1862–63, was given a manuscript of part of Tannhäuser (Wagner demanded it back in 1875), and in January 1863 played Wagner his Handel Variations; the meeting was cordial.

sources.title: War of the Romantics (Wikipedia): “The conservatives’ manifesto”
Johannes Brahms (Wikipedia): “Wagner and his circle”

edges.title: Berlioz “reads and re-reads” the Tristan prelude, baffled

works.from: Wagner, Tristan und Isolde, Act I prelude (concert at the Salle Ventadour, February 1860)
works.to: Berlioz, review of Wagner’s concerts, Journal des Débats, 9 February 1860

edges.claim: Wagner’s Paris concerts of January–February 1860 included the Tristan prelude, and [[berlioz]] reviewed them in the Journal des Débats on 9 February. He describes a slow piece that starts pianissimo, swells to fortissimo and falls back, with “no theme other than a sort of chromatic moaning” over dissonances whose long appoggiaturas replace the real note of the harmony. He says he has read the “strange page” again and again, listened with full attention, and still cannot tell what the composer means. Wagner, who had sent him the Tristan score early in 1860, answered with an open letter in the same paper on 22 February.

sources.title: Berlioz, “Concerts de Richard Wagner”, Journal des Débats, 9 February 1860 (The Hector Berlioz Website)
sources.locator: paragraph on the Tristan et Iseult introduction

edges.title: Brahms builds twenty-five variations on a Handel aria

works.from: Handel, Harpsichord Suite No. 1 in B♭, HWV 434: aria in the third movement (Walsh, 1733)
works.to: Brahms, Variations and Fugue on a Theme by Handel, Op. 24 (September 1861)

edges.claim: [[brahms]] took the theme of Op. 24 from an aria in the third movement of Handel’s Suite No. 1 in B♭, HWV 434, and owned a copy of the 1733 first edition. He wrote the work in a single stretch in September 1861, twenty-five variations and a fugue, and gave it to [[clara-schumann]] on her forty-second birthday, 13 September. She first played it in Hamburg on 7 December 1861 and repeated it soon afterwards in Leipzig.

edges.title: Saint-Saëns brings Schumann, Liszt and Wagner to Fauré’s school

works.from: Saint-Saëns’s piano classes at the École Niedermeyer, Paris, from 1861
works.to: Fauré’s early mélodies and piano works

edges.claim: Gabriel Fauré boarded at the École Niedermeyer in Paris from the age of nine, trained as church organist and choirmaster; Louis Niedermeyer himself taught piano, plainsong and composition. When Niedermeyer died in March 1861, saint-saens took charge of piano studies and introduced the pupils to contemporary music, including that of Schumann, Liszt and Wagner. Fauré recalled this in old age, and Saint-Saëns remained a lifelong friend; in 1877 he took Fauré to Weimar to meet [[liszt]].

edges.title: Rimsky-Korsakov learns orchestration from Berlioz’s Treatise

works.from: Berlioz, Grand traité d’instrumentation et d’orchestration modernes (1844)
works.to: Rimsky-Korsakov, Symphony No. 1 (1861–65); Principles of Orchestration (preface 1891)

edges.claim: Inexperienced in orchestration when he began his First Symphony in 1861, [[rimsky-korsakov]] turned to Hector Berlioz’s treatise as well as to the advice of Balakirev. Thirty years later, in the 1891 preface to his own Principles of Orchestration, he named Berlioz first among the colourists, with Glinka, Liszt and Wagner, who had brought orchestral colour to its zenith. He told students that Weber, Mendelssohn, Berlioz, Glinka, Wagner, Liszt and modern French and Russian composers would be their best guides.

edges.title: Wagner’s Beckmesser began as “Veit Hanslich”

works.from: Eduard Hanslick, Vienna’s leading critic (On the Musically Beautiful, 1854)
works.to: Wagner, Die Meistersinger von Nürnberg: the Merker, then Beckmesser (prose draft 1861; reading in Vienna, 23 November 1862)

edges.claim: When [[wagner]] turned the Meistersinger prose draft into a libretto in Vienna in 1861, he named the pedantic town clerk who marks the singers’ faults “Veit Hanslich”, an open allusion to the Vienna critic Eduard Hanslick. By the time Wagner first read the text aloud in Vienna on 23 November 1862, with Hanslick among the listeners, the name had become Sixtus Beckmesser. Hanslick, who championed Schumann and [[brahms]] against Wagner and [[liszt]], knew he was the target.
edges.note: The draft name “Veit Hanslich” and Hanslick’s presence at the 1862 reading are documented; that the finished Beckmesser caricatures Hanslick is an interpretation, and general reference works still say only that it is “sometimes claimed”.

sources.title: Sixtus Beckmesser (wagner200.com, in German): draft name and the reading of 23 November 1862

edges.title: Tchaikovsky attends all six Wagner concerts in St Petersburg

works.from: Wagner conducting in St Petersburg, 1863: Tristan prelude and Liebestod, Beethoven symphonies and others
works.to: Tchaikovsky’s Bayreuth reports of 1876 and his later verdict on Wagner

edges.claim: In 1863, in his first year at the Conservatory, [[tchaikovsky]] attended all six concerts that [[wagner]] gave in St Petersburg. They included the Prelude and “Liebestod” from Tristan und Isolde and Beethoven’s Third and Fifth to Eighth symphonies; Tchaikovsky counted the experience among the most memorable of his life. In 1875 he heard Klindworth play through the whole Ring in piano transcription, and in August 1876 he reached Bayreuth for the first Rheingold as correspondent for a Moscow newspaper.

edges.title: Balakirev guides and premieres Rimsky-Korsakov’s First Symphony

works.from: Balakirev’s guidance of the young naval cadet, 1861–65
works.to: Rimsky-Korsakov, Symphony No. 1, Op. 1 (premiered by Balakirev, December 1865)

edges.claim: [[rimsky-korsakov]] wrote his Symphony No. 1 between 1861 and 1865 under the guidance of Balakirev, who conducted its first performance at a Free Music School concert in December 1865. The composer acknowledged Schumann’s Manfred Overture and Third Symphony, Glinka’s Prince Kholmsky and Balakirev’s King Lear overture as models. He later wrote that he felt his own ignorance but was convinced that Balakirev knew everything, and that Balakirev cleverly concealed from him and the others of “The Five” the insufficiency of his own training.

edges.title: Mussorgsky sets Gogol’s Marriage as Dargomyzhsky set Pushkin

works.from: Dargomyzhsky, The Stone Guest, Pushkin’s text set “just as it stands” (begun 1866)
works.to: Mussorgsky, Zhenitba (Marriage), after Gogol’s comedy (begun 1868; unfinished)

edges.claim: [[mussorgsky]]’s idea of setting Gogol’s comedy Marriage came from the advice and example of Alexander Dargomyzhsky, who in 1866 began The Stone Guest, declaring that Pushkin’s text would be set “just as it stands, so that the inner truth of the text should not be distorted”. It replaced the division between aria and recitative with a continuous, syllabic but lyrically heightened declamation. In 1868 Mussorgsky quickly set the first eleven scenes of Gogol’s prose, catching the natural accents of its humdrum dialogue; he left the work unfinished.

sources.title: The Marriage (Mussorgsky) (Wikipedia): composition history

edges.title: Mussorgsky turns Pushkin’s Boris Godunov into an opera

works.from: Pushkin, Boris Godunov (written 1825, published 1831); Karamzin, History of the Russian State
works.to: Mussorgsky, Boris Godunov (original version 1869; revised 1872; premiere 27 January 1874)

edges.claim: In the autumn of 1868 the historian Vladimir Nikolsky suggested to [[mussorgsky]] an opera on Pushkin’s “dramatic chronicle” Boris Godunov, and Lyudmila Shestakova gave him a volume of Pushkin’s plays interleaved with blank pages; he began his own libretto in October. He finished the score in December 1869, and the Imperial Theatres rejected it on 10 February 1871 by six votes to one, ostensibly for lack of a major female role. The revised version of 1872 was first performed at the Mariinsky Theatre on 27 January 1874.

sources.title: Boris Godunov (opera) (Wikipedia): composition history; rejection of the 1869 version

edges.title: Balakirev sets Tchaikovsky’s Romeo and Juliet in order

works.from: Balakirev’s letters and his overture King Lear (as formal model), 1869
works.to: Tchaikovsky, Romeo and Juliet, fantasy overture (first version 1869; dedicated to Balakirev)

edges.claim: Balakirev suggested the subject of Romeo and Juliet to [[tchaikovsky]] when they met in Moscow in the summer of 1869, after criticising Tchaikovsky’s Fatum frankly. He sent a plan describing the type of music for each section, with advice on keys, and held up his own King Lear overture as a model. Tchaikovsky wrote on 14 October 1869 that he was “played out completely”; “abusive letters” from Balakirev followed, and on 24 October he reported he was writing the overture. The work is dedicated to Balakirev, though the inscription was left off the first printed scores.

edges.title: Verdi annotates Lohengrin at Bologna, November 1871

works.from: Wagner, Lohengrin, Italian premiere at the Teatro Comunale, Bologna, 1 November 1871
works.to: Verdi’s pencilled notes in a vocal score, 9 November 1871

edges.claim: Angelo Mariani conducted the first performance of a Wagner opera in Italy, Lohengrin at the Teatro Comunale of Bologna, on 1 November 1871. On 9 November [[verdi]] attended and annotated a copy of the vocal score with his impressions and opinions; it was almost certainly his first exposure to Wagner’s music. In 1887 a German visitor recorded him as saying there was much to admire in Tannhäuser and Lohengrin, but that in his later operas Wagner seemed to overstep the limits of what music can express.

edges.title: Bruckner dedicates his Third Symphony to Wagner

works.from: Wagner, Die Walküre, Tristan und Isolde, Lohengrin, Tannhäuser
works.to: Bruckner, Symphony No. 3 in D minor, WAB 103 (1873 version)

edges.claim: In September 1873, before the Third Symphony was finished, [[bruckner]] visited [[wagner]], whom he had first met at the Munich premiere of Tristan und Isolde in 1865. He showed Wagner his Second and Third Symphonies and asked him to choose; Wagner chose the Third, and Bruckner dedicated it to him. The 1873 score quoted Wagner’s Die Walküre and Tristan in the first movement and Lohengrin and Walküre in the Adagio; after the Vienna premiere of 1877 failed, Bruckner’s revisions removed most of these quotations.

edges.title: Mussorgsky walks through Hartmann’s memorial exhibition

works.from: Viktor Hartmann’s drawings and designs, memorial exhibition, St Petersburg, February–March 1874
works.to: Mussorgsky, Pictures at an Exhibition, piano suite (composed 2–22 June 1874)

edges.claim: Viktor Hartmann, an architect and designer, died suddenly on 4 August 1873, aged thirty-nine. The critic Vladimir Stasov helped organise a memorial exhibition of over 400 of his works at the Imperial Academy of Arts in February and March 1874; [[mussorgsky]] lent the two pictures Hartmann had given him in 1868 and viewed the show. He composed Pictures at an Exhibition between 2 and 22 June 1874 and dedicated it to Stasov. “Ballet of the Unhatched Chicks” answers Hartmann’s costume sketch of canary chicks for the ballet Trilby (1871).

edges.title: Brahms’s finale tune answers Beethoven’s Ode to Joy

works.from: Beethoven, Symphony No. 9, finale: “Ode to Joy” theme (1824)
works.to: Brahms, Symphony No. 1, finale: main Allegro theme (first performed 4 November 1876)

edges.claim: The broad tune that [[brahms]] gives the strings in the C-major Allegro of his First Symphony finale resembles the “Ode to Joy” theme of [[beethoven]]’s Ninth. When this was pointed out to him he is reported to have answered “Any ass can see that”. In 1877 the conductor Hans von Bülow called the symphony “Beethoven’s Tenth”; it was first played at Karlsruhe on 4 November 1876 under Felix Otto Dessoff.

edges.title: Tchaikovsky sets Pushkin’s own verses in Eugene Onegin

works.from: Pushkin, Eugene Onegin, verse novel (1825–32)
works.to: Tchaikovsky, Eugene Onegin, “lyrical scenes”, Op. 24 (premiere 29 March 1879)

edges.claim: In May 1877 the singer Yelizaveta Lavrovskaya proposed to [[tchaikovsky]] an opera on Pushkin’s verse novel. He doubted the plot was strong enough, but after a sleepless night embraced the idea and drafted the scenario in a single night. With Konstantin Shilovsky’s minor help he used original verses from Pushkin and chose scenes from the characters’ emotional lives, calling the work “lyrical scenes”. It was first performed at the Maly Theatre in Moscow on 29 March 1879.

edges.title: Brahms recommends Dvořák to Simrock; Slavonic Dances follow

works.from: Brahms, Hungarian Dances (piano four hands) and his referral to Simrock
works.to: Dvořák, Slavonic Dances, Op. 46 (1878; orchestrated for Simrock)

edges.claim: [[dvorak]] won the Austrian State Prize in 1874, 1876 and 1877. [[brahms]], on the committee, referred him to his own publisher, Fritz Simrock, who first issued the Moravian Duets and then asked for something dance-like. Unsure how to begin, Dvořák took Brahms’s Hungarian Dances as a model, but only as a model: Brahms used real Hungarian folk melodies, whereas Dvořák mostly used the characteristic rhythms of Bohemian folk dances with melodies of his own. The Op. 46 set, written for piano four hands, was orchestrated soon after at Simrock’s request.

edges.title: Brahms’s Fourth ends on Bach’s Cantata 150 bass

works.from: Bach, Cantata Nach dir, Herr, verlanget mich, BWV 150, closing chaconne
works.to: Brahms, Symphony No. 4 in E minor, Op. 98, finale: passacaglia

edges.claim: The finale of [[brahms]]’s Fourth Symphony is a passacaglia on an eight-bar theme adapted from the closing chaconne of Bach’s Cantata 150, which was then unpublished. Brahms added a leading tone to Bach’s bass and regularised its rhythm into eight dotted half notes that rise from the tonic E to the dominant B, drop an octave and return. The theme is stated thirty times, always eight bars long, before the coda begins at bar 253.

edges.title: Rimsky-Korsakov rebuilds Mussorgsky’s Bald Mountain in 1886

works.from: Mussorgsky, St John’s Eve on Bald Mountain (1867); Mlada (1872); The Fair at Sorochyntsi (1880)
works.to: Rimsky-Korsakov, Night on Bald Mountain (completed and published 1886)

edges.claim: [[mussorgsky]] finished St John’s Eve on Bald Mountain on 23 June 1867, but Balakirev refused to perform it, so he reused the music in the collaborative opera-ballet Mlada (1872) and in The Fair at Sorochyntsi (1880). After Mussorgsky’s death in 1881 [[rimsky-korsakov]] made his own version, completed and published in 1886, and wrote that its form, modulations and orchestration had resisted him for two years. He conducted the first performance at the Russian Symphony Concerts in St Petersburg on 15 October 1886 and made substantial “corrections” to melody, harmony, rhythm and dynamics.

edges.title: Tchaikovsky orchestrates Mozart piano pieces as Mozartiana

works.from: Mozart: Gigue, K. 574; Minuet, K. 355; Liszt’s transcription of Ave verum corpus; variations on a theme of Gluck
works.to: Tchaikovsky, Suite No. 4 “Mozartiana”, Op. 61 (June–July 1887)

edges.claim: [[tchaikovsky]] told his diary in 1886 that he loved Beethoven as one fears God but loved Mozart “as a musical Christ”. At sixteen or seventeen he had heard Don Giovanni almost by chance and called it a revelation; on 17 May 1884 he wrote “Played Mozart and was in raptures. Thought about a suite from Mozart.” In June and July 1887 he orchestrated four pieces, among them the Gigue, K. 574, and the Minuet, K. 355, as the Suite No. 4, which he described to his publisher as “the old given a contemporary treatment”.

edges.title: Rimsky-Korsakov takes Scheherazade from the Thousand and One Nights

works.from: The Thousand and One Nights; the story of Prince Ajib
works.to: Rimsky-Korsakov, Scheherazade, Op. 35 (1888; premiere 28 October 1888)

edges.claim: [[rimsky-korsakov]] composed Scheherazade in 1888 on themes from the Thousand and One Nights. After weighing the opinions of Anatoly Lyadov and others, and his own dislike of a too-definite programme, he settled on thematic headings such as “The Young Prince and the Young Princess”, deliberately vague, though the finale’s epigraph does refer to the adventure of Prince Ajib. In a later edition he dropped the titles altogether, wanting listeners to hear oriental-flavoured symphonic music that suggests fairy-tale adventure.

edges.title: Fauré’s Requiem leaves out the Dies irae

works.from: The Requiem sequence Dies irae (Gregorian chant; setting tradition)
works.to: Fauré, Requiem, Op. 48 (1887–90; first version 1888)

edges.claim: [[faure]]’s Requiem sets seven movements and omits the full sequence Dies irae, keeping only its closing section, the Pie Jesu; he followed a French Baroque tradition in this, did not set the Benedictus, and added two texts from the burial service, Libera me and In paradisum. He wrote that everything he could muster of religious illusion went into the work, which is “dominated from beginning to end by a very human feeling of faith in eternal rest”. The first version was sung at a funeral at the Madeleine in 1888.

sources.title: Requiem (Fauré) (Wikipedia): Text; history; Fauré’s own description

edges.title: Fauré and Messager turn the Ring into a quadrille

works.from: Wagner, Der Ring des Nibelungen, as heard by Fauré and Messager at Cologne, Munich, London and Bayreuth
works.to: Fauré and Messager, Souvenirs de Bayreuth, quadrille for piano four hands (c. 1888; published 1930)

edges.claim: From 1878 [[faure]] and his former pupil André Messager travelled to hear Wagner: Das Rheingold and Die Walküre at Cologne, the whole Ring at Munich and London, and Die Meistersinger and Parsifal at Bayreuth. Their joint Souvenirs de Bayreuth, a “fantasy in the form of a quadrille on favourite themes from the Ring”, was composed probably in 1888 and published in 1930. It grew from improvisations at Marguerite de Saint-Marceaux’s salon, which Colette recalled; Fauré admired Wagner yet is described as one of the few of his generation to escape his musical influence.

edges.title: Hoffmann’s Nutcracker reaches Tchaikovsky through Dumas

works.from: E. T. A. Hoffmann, Nussknacker und Mausekönig (1816), in Dumas’s Histoire d’un casse-noisette (1845)
works.to: Tchaikovsky, The Nutcracker, Op. 71 (February 1891–April 1892)

edges.claim: The libretto of [[tchaikovsky]]’s last ballet was compiled by Ivan Vsevolozhsky and Marius Petipa from Alexandre Dumas’s Histoire d’un Casse-Noisette (1845), which Dumas adapted from E. T. A. Hoffmann’s Der Nußknacker und Mausekönig (1816). Tchaikovsky wrote and orchestrated the score between February 1891 and April 1892, and drew a concert suite of eight numbers from it. The Christmas Eve setting is in eighteenth-century Germany, in the home of President Silberhaus.

edges.title: Burleigh sings spirituals to Dvořák in New York

works.from: Spirituals sung by Harry T. Burleigh at the National Conservatory, New York
works.to: Dvořák, Symphony No. 9 “From the New World”, Largo (premiere 16 December 1893)

edges.claim: While [[dvorak]] directed the National Conservatory in New York, the African-American student Harry T. Burleigh sang traditional spirituals to him; Burleigh said Dvořák absorbed their “spirit” before writing his own melodies. Dvořák is said to have given the Largo’s main theme to the cor anglais rather than the clarinet because it reminded him of Burleigh’s voice. In the New York Herald of 1893 he said the future music of America must be founded on what are called Negro melodies. The first movement’s closing theme resembles “Swing Low, Sweet Chariot”, but Dvořák wrote his own themes.
edges.note: Burleigh’s role as singer and Dvořák’s published statements about Negro melodies are documented; the cor anglais anecdote is reported as hearsay (“was said to have”), and Dvořák denied quoting existing tunes, so the resemblance to “Swing Low, Sweet Chariot” remains an observation, not a documented borrowing.

sources.title: Symphony No. 9 (Dvořák) (Wikipedia): Largo; Influences; the New York Herald statements

edges.title: Dvořák calls the Largo a Hiawatha study

works.from: Longfellow, The Song of Hiawatha (1855)
works.to: Dvořák, Symphony No. 9, Largo and Scherzo

edges.claim: In the New York Herald of 15 December 1893, the day before the premiere at Carnegie Hall, [[dvorak]] said that he regarded the second movement as a “sketch or study” for a later cantata or opera on Longfellow’s Hiawatha, and that the Scherzo was suggested by the scene of the feast where the Indians dance. No such cantata or opera was written. The symphony was commissioned by the New York Philharmonic and first played on 16 December 1893 under Anton Seidl.
